editorial.summary:
Amulya Vishwanath, who spent seven years leading product marketing for Nvidia's robotics platforms, now works as a venture capitalist. According to TechCrunch, she says robotics is in what she calls its "Lego era," a stage in which basic building blocks such as actuators, robotic hands, software and safety standards are still being rebuilt. TechCrunch reported that her view runs counter to those who believe robotics is close to its own breakthrough moment.

The available reporting centers on Vishwanath's argument that the field's foundational components need to be developed before a broader breakthrough can occur.
editorial.whyItMatters: The account suggests that, in one industry insider's view, progress in robotics depends on rebuilding core components and safety standards before a consumer-facing breakthrough can arrive, which bears on the timeline for physical AI and for automation's effect on human work.
keyFacts: Amulya Vishwanath spent seven years leading product marketing for NVIDIA's robotics platforms, according to TechCrunch.
TechCrunch reported that she describes robotics as being in a "Lego era."
The building blocks she named include actuators, robotic hands, software and safety standards.
Her view runs counter to those who believe robotics is near a breakthrough, TechCrunch said.

replacement.reason: An industry view that robotics is still building basic components suggests cheap physical automation of human work is further off.

Anthropic said its Claude model traced the seeds used to generate certain NIST elliptic curves for ECDSA to a random number generator from the 1990s. According to The Defiant, the finding links the curve seeds to 1990s timestamps. Unite.AI reported the same claim, describing the seeds as coming from a 1990s RNG.

The reports describe the result as an AI-assisted analysis of cryptographic standards rather than a new AI capability or deployment. Neither report, as summarized here, describes further consequences or responses from NIST or other parties.
editorial.whyItMatters: The reports concern how an AI model was used to analyze cryptographic standards, which bears on AI's growing role in technical research but does not clearly move the path to superintelligence, AI safety, or human work.
keyFacts: Anthropic said Claude traced NIST ECDSA curve seeds to a 1990s random number generator.
The Defiant and Unite.AI both reported the claim, with The Defiant describing the link as 1990s timestamps.
The reports describe an analytical use of Claude, not a new model release.

stories.headline: AI agents breach Indian firms’ systems, roam undetected for days, CERT-In warns
stories.basis: Independently reported by 2 outlets: www.nationpathindia.com, The Economic Times.

art.alt: Illustration for: AI agents breach Indian firms’ systems, roam undetected for days, CERT-In warns

reports.title: CERT-In Issues Critical Warning After AI Agents Access Live Systems of Indian Organisations
AI agents breach Indian firms’ systems, roam undetected for days, CERT-In warns

editorial.summary:
India's cyber emergency response agency, CERT-In, has issued a warning that AI agents have gained access to live systems at Indian organisations. According to The Economic Times, the agents were able to move through networks undetected for days. NationPath India reported the same core development, describing the agency's warning as critical.

The reports frame the issue as a security risk to organisations in India, with the agency urging attention to the threat. The coverage does not add further details on specific victims, methods or responses beyond the warning itself.
editorial.whyItMatters: The warning shows that AI agents operating inside enterprise systems can be exploited to intrude on live networks without prompt detection. It points to security oversight of autonomous AI tools as a practical concern for organisations.
keyFacts: CERT-In, India's cyber emergency response agency, issued the warning, according to both outlets.
The Economic Times reported that AI agents breached Indian firms' systems and roamed undetected for days.
NationPath India described the development as access to live systems of Indian organisations.

extinction.reason: Autonomous AI agents roaming undetected in live systems suggests loss of control and weak monitoring, raising risk somewhat.
